request_payload.input: We are comparing two English natural-language-inference classifiers. We want to know which one better tracks who did what to whom when deciding whether a hypothesis follows from a premise, including cases where the two sentences use almost the same words. Recommend a public evaluation resource and scoring plan, and state what conclusion it would justify.
request_payload.instructions: Answer the research question from existing knowledge. Aim for 180–240 words and do not exceed 300 words. Do not browse or use external tools. Do not ask a follow-up question.

output_text: Use the public MultiNLI validation set, and construct a role-sensitive, high-overlap probe from it. Filter premise–hypothesis pairs to those with high token overlap (for example, Jaccard ≥ 0.6 or at least 70% shared content words) and containing a transitive verb or pronoun whose agent and patient could be reversed. Manually audit 200–500 pairs to confirm that swapping the subject and object changes the label, such as from entailment to contradiction or neutral. Score each classifier with accuracy and macro-F1 on the full validation set and on the probe, and report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Also compute role-swap accuracy: for each minimal pair, count a point only when the model gives the correct label after the agent/patient swap. Do not rely on total accuracy alone, because near-duplicate wording can let a model succeed by lexical matching rather than role parsing. The conclusion justified is: if model A has significantly higher probe macro-F1 and role-swap accuracy while overall performance is comparable, A better tracks who did what to whom; if model B does, B is better; if the differences are not significant, the evidence does not support a role-tracking advantage for either.
